halvard: Halvard's collectors count the grain before we know whether the harvest will feed us. I would like him to spend one winter eating what he leaves behind.
I have stopped setting aside the crown's share. The first extra sack goes to anyone whose cupboard is bare.
history: Millwood's harvests
Neighbours used to bring their grain to the mill together. If a cart broke, everybody behind it got down to help.
Did they mind waiting?
Of course. They complained all the way through the repair. Being neighbours did not require being cheerful about it.

halvard: The crown wants sound timber and pays for scraps. I mend the village fences first, whatever the order on the paper says.
We can choose what to build with our own wood. Hettie wants the sheds repaired; I would like a new bridge rail before somebody falls in.
history: The old millwork
Older repairs in Millwood often used different kinds of timber. People brought what they could spare.
Does that make them weaker?
Not if the wood is sound and the joints are suited to it. A careful repair need not match in color.

halvard: His men ask who crosses this bridge. I tell them about the fish. They have yet to notice I am much better informed about people.
For once, a visitor can cross without being questioned. I might even put down my rod long enough to welcome them.
history: Life around the bridge
People stopped on this bridge to exchange news long before anyone put up a noticeboard.
You were listening even then?
I was fishing. If people insist on conducting history beside my line, I cannot be expected to close my ears.

halvard: I took an oath to keep the road safe. Lately my orders mostly concern stopping people who have done nothing wrong.
I still have a spear and a duty to the people on this road. I would like the next order I follow to serve both.
You can make a frightened recruit obey almost anything. A king ought to be ashamed of relying on that.
Some of my men are waiting for someone to tell them what to think. I have told them to begin by listening to the people they frightened.
I owe my rank to the crown. That makes speaking against Halvard difficult; it does not make every order right.
Taking off the badge would be easy. Living among the people who remember it will take rather more courage.
I remember the riders before Halvard's account became the only one people dared repeat. Keep asking who lived through a story, Corin, and who profits from it.
He spent so long trying to be the end of our history. Now we have the difficult work of teaching what happened without raising another generation on hatred.
history: The roads before Wingfall
The riders helped keep the roads open. Carters and masons did the ordinary work of maintaining them; those names rarely reached the songs.
Was travel easy then?
Easier in some seasons than others. Do not let nostalgia persuade you we never had mud or a broken wheel.

halvard: When soldiers come, everyone goes quiet. I do not understand a king who wants his arrival to sound like that.
We heard laughter coming down the path. I went to look instead of hiding under the caps.

dd: The caps are trembling all along the path. They can feel your dragon walking.
Corin: Are we hurting them?
Pip: No. Just give the little ones room. They have never felt footsteps like his.
dd2: The caps have settled since you stopped walking. I think they are listening to his breathing.

halvard: I remember the forest before his reign. He speaks as though anything older than his crown must belong beneath it.
Roots outlast a man's commands. I am relieved that the people above them have been given another chance as well.
history: The forest before the crown
Young trees spread into clearings, old trees fell, and the rings grew beneath both. Humans gave those changes dates. We remember which roots returned.
Do you remember the riders?
I remember dragons crossing above the canopy. What their riders said to one another belonged to a world I could not hear.

dd: I saw dragons above this valley when I was young. I never expected to stand this close to one.
Corin: He hatched near Millwood. Everything is new to him.
Mycella: Then let him look. There is no need to hurry every first meeting.
dd2: Keep your young companion on the clear path. The deep hollow hides soft ground beneath the caps.

halvard: A patrol cut through the young caps to save a few steps. When I objected, they showed me the king's mark.
I have planted where the patrol cut through. It will take several wet seasons to cover the damage, but nobody is stopping me.

dd2: Your dragon will attract the crown's attention. Do not assume a small patrol is the only one watching the road.

halvard: His men stamp the ground and call it theirs. I would trust them more if they noticed what they were crushing.
The ground has not forgotten the boots. Give the little caps time; quiet does not immediately feel safe.

d: The northern ground carries every footstep a long way. Stay on the firm path; the quiet patches can be soft beneath the grass.
dd: Your companion walks lightly for something with such large feet. The caps felt you coming before I saw either of you.
Corin: He hatched near Millwood. He is still learning where to put those feet.
Truffle: Give him room to turn. The new shoots are easy to miss.
dd2: I can tell your steps from his now. Yours hurry; his keep stopping beside interesting things.
dv2: I remember feeling your young companion's steps along our path. I am glad you have both come back to walk it again.

halvard: Halvard believes being king means nobody may refuse him. My ring would take this crown away if I stopped hearing them.
I hope your people choose who speaks for them carefully. Being rid of a cruel ruler is a beginning, not the whole task.
history: How the ring chooses a voice
We listen until the quietest concern has been heard. Whoever wears the crown must remember the concerns, not merely the loudest speakers.
Does that take a long time?
Often. We lose more time repairing a decision made before anyone understood its cost.
afterGift: Walk gently through the ring, Corin. You are a guest here, and the little ones are learning what that means.
gift: Take a spore of the deep ring. Wear it, and defeating an enemy will restore a little of your strength.
Corin: Why give it to me?
You have roads still to walk. We would like to hear what you found when you return.

halvard: Travellers used to ask whether my fire was warm. Now they ask whether I have seen a patrol. That is what his peace has done for business.
People are lingering over breakfast again. Yesterday two strangers argued about the best road simply because both roads were open.
history: Travellers' camps
A camp became useful when people knew they could find water and company there. The fire mattered less than the certainty someone would tend it.
What kept them coming back?
Hearing that the last traveller reached the next town. News of a safe road is good advertising.

dd: A dragon at my camp. I will have trouble persuading the next guests that I did not invent this.
Corin: He is better company than most people expect.
dd2: There is room by the fire for you. Your companion can rest on the open ground beside the camp.

halvard: Father dressed stone for royal wagons until his fingers would not straighten. The clerk recorded the blocks, never his name.
If the town repairs those walls, I want the masons named. People ought to know whose hands kept the rain off them.

dd2: It is good to see something young and curious here. Give your dragon room; people will want to stop and look.

halvard: A royal seal does not keep a mine roof up. I wish the men who set the quotas would come below before demanding another cart.
I want the crews deciding when a gallery is unsafe. We have had enough courage praised by people standing in daylight.
history: The older galleries
The mine grew a passage at a time. Each crew left marks so the next could tell sound work from a place nobody had tested.
Can we trust those marks now?
Treat them as someone's last report, not a promise. Water and time can undo a careful man's work.

halvard: The inn has had fewer travellers since the king's patrols started stopping people on the roads. I miss hearing where everyone has been.
People are planning journeys again. I have promised Maren I will help get the spare rooms ready.
history: Helping at the inn
I used to carry baskets from the market for Maren. Now she trusts me to choose what goes in them.
What do you bring back?
Bread, fruit, clean linen. And usually one thing we did not need because it smelled too good to leave.
bramble: Oh, Bramble! He waits outside the inn when he smells breakfast. His owner is Rowan, the hunter. You will find him at the Copper Cup in northern Thornwell.

d: Linna: Welcome to Thornwell. If you need a bed, Maren keeps the inn.
Corin: Do you work there?
Linna: I help with errands. It is a good excuse to see everyone in town.
dd: Linna: Is that little dragon travelling with you?
Corin: He is. His name is Aurelius.
Linna: Well, welcome to Thornwell, both of you. I will keep my bread basket out of his reach.
dd2: Linna: He is keeping close to you. You must be getting on well.
away: Linna: I heard you have a dragon travelling with you. Is he waiting outside?
Corin: Yes. There is more room for him there.
Linna: Sensible. Most rooms here were built with rather smaller guests in mind.
dv: Linna: You are back! Maren will want to hear everything. Come to the inn when you have had a rest.
dv2: Linna: I like hearing carts on the road again. It means people feel safe enough to visit.

halvard: I treat the king's men when they come to my counter. I wish he cared as much about the injuries he sends them home with.
I will still treat anyone who needs help. Ending his rule should mean fewer wounds, not choosing different people to neglect.

dd: He seems alert. Let me know if your dragon needs tending; I would rather hear about a small injury than a neglected one.
dd2: The king's men have been buying salve for burns. Seeing your companion makes me wonder what they have been sent after.

halvard: The king's collectors take the best produce before my customers even see it. I still have to explain why the good apples are gone.
I can sell what we grow without setting half of it aside for the crown. The market feels like ours again.
bramble: Bramble knows my stall. Rowan always buys him an apple slice. Look for the hunter at the Copper Cup in Thornwell.

d: Bevan: Apples, carrots, and whatever looked good in the garden this morning.
Corin: Those are fine apples.
Bevan: Try one before you choose. A shiny skin is not everything.
dd: Bevan: Your dragon is very interested in my baskets.
Corin: I think he is hoping there is meat in one.
Bevan: Only vegetables here. I am afraid I will have to disappoint him.
away: Bevan: I heard about your dragon. I hope you packed more than apples for him.
dv: Bevan: We are keeping the best of the harvest this year. You helped make that possible, Corin.
dv2: Bevan: There is enough here to share. That feels better than any victory speech.

halvard: I make drinks for anyone who asks, but the king's patrols have a habit of expecting theirs for nothing.
For the first time in years, a uniform at the market does not make everyone fall quiet. I could get used to that.
bramble: That is Rowan's dog. The hunter buys a bottle from me when he is passing through. Try the Copper Cup on the north side of town; that is where he stops when he is home.

d: Isolde: Cider, berry cordial, and fresh water. What will it be?
Corin: Just looking, thank you.
Isolde: No hurry. Find me when you are thirsty.
dd: Isolde: Oh! Is your dragon thirsty after the journey?
Corin: Probably. He is always happy to stop for a drink.
Isolde: There is plenty of fresh water in town. Help yourselves.
dd2: Isolde: Has your companion had his drink? A long road makes thirsty work.
away: Isolde: I heard you are travelling with a dragon. Does he drink from a bucket?
Corin: If it is a big enough bucket.
Isolde: I had better keep the large one handy, then.
dv: Isolde: A drink for the road, Corin? After what you have done, this one is on me.
dv2: Isolde: The market is busy again. I have not enjoyed running out of cider this much in years.

halvard: A thirsty soldier gets water here. His king does not get to claim the well because I offered it.
Our well will stay open to travellers. I would like that kindness to survive whoever arrives carrying the next banner.
history: Sandspire's cisterns
Routes through the dry country followed places where water could be stored. A market could grow only when travellers trusted the next drink would be there.
Was your father's cistern part of that?
He repaired and lined what others had begun. I am proud of his work without needing him to have invented water.

halvard: The crown takes its cut at each stop, then blames traders when spice costs more. My mother could name every hand between the sack and the customer.
I can tell a customer the price without apologising for a levy I never chose. It feels like recovering my own voice.
history: The caravan roads
Goods travelled farther than most people who bought them. A sack could change hands several times before anyone here opened it.
How do you know its history?
Marks on the wrapping, a familiar knot, a trader who remembers the last owner. Not every useful record lives in a book.

halvard: A royal order cannot tell a camel when it is too tired to walk. I have lost good animals to officers who insisted otherwise.
We can let the caravan rest through the heat. I wish the animals we buried could have had that choice.
My daughter works late to cover the levy. Halvard would call that loyalty if he ever bothered to ask why her lamp is burning.
She put her loom away before supper yesterday. We had a whole conversation with both her hands resting in her lap.
I used to tell my sons a careful trader could make a life here. Each new demand from Cinderhold makes that promise harder to keep.
Perhaps my boys will still choose the coast. I want them leaving from curiosity, not because I could offer them no future here.
He wants beautiful glass in his halls and cheap glass on his invoices. I have an opinion of his taste, but a worse one of his honesty.
I would like my next fine piece to sit in a house whose owner saved for it. I am tired of calling an order an honour.
afterGift: The glassworkers of Sandspire and Forgewick could argue all afternoon. I will spare you that unless you mean to buy a cup.
gift: Take this fire rune, Corin. Wear it and every third sword swing will strike with flame.
Corin: You are giving it to me?
A traveller may have more use for it than a glassworker. I have a furnace when I need heat.

halvard: The collectors count the kids before they are weaned. Even a goat knows better than to take everything at once.
I am keeping two young does this year. Freedom, in my yard, begins with a herd large enough to survive a bad season.
A man in a warm hall can decree a larger catch. He cannot persuade the sea to give one. The hungry people end up at my pot.
I would like to cook because people enjoy my stew, instead of because it is the only meal they can stretch to.
Royal celebrations always wanted music, but payment was supposedly another clerk's concern. A landlord does not accept applause in place of rent.
I kept notes of the performances the crown never paid for. I may never collect the money, but I will not pretend the work was a gift.

d: Potions for the road. Tell me what you need before you open anything; I prefer my counter in one piece.

halvard: Every checkpoint has a different account of what the king requires. Somehow every account ends with my purse being lighter.
I can count my costs before I leave home again. That may sound dull. Dull is an excellent condition for a trader.
He taxes what comes ashore without sharing the risk of bringing it in. I would like to see him explain that bargain to a storm.
The harbour needs repairs before anybody orders a celebration. I hope we spend our first free money on something that lasts.
history: How Coralmere grew
Boats brought catches, goods and people who thought they would stay one night. Some repaired a net, took work, and stopped counting the nights.
Is that how your family came here?
My aunt came looking for work. The grand history would call her a settler. She called it finding somewhere the rent could be paid.

halvard: When winter closes the roads, decrees do not feed us. Neighbours do. I know which of those I trust.
I am glad he is gone. I still count the stores each evening; being free will not make winter shorter.
I have heard enough proclamations to know when someone is trying to sell me hunger as duty. Let me eat before asking for my gratitude.
For years I lowered my voice before complaining. I still catch myself doing it. It is a habit I will enjoy losing.
I can play a tune he has forbidden without singing a word. That is the small amount of disobedience I can carry in public.
I want the old words back as well as the notes. People should get to decide which verses they remember.
A royal hunting boundary means little to a hungry family. I take what the woods can spare and try not to meet a patrol coming home.
I hope we keep limits on the hunt, even now. Halvard being gone does not mean the woods can feed every careless appetite.
I have helped people through storms while his officers argued over travel papers. A stamp is poor shelter.
We can mend the road without waiting for someone far away to admit it is broken. Bring willing hands; that is permission enough for me.
history: Hollybeck's winter customs
People left lamps in windows so a neighbour caught outside could find a door. Later we began keeping spare gloves there too.
For anyone who knocked?
Anyone cold enough to knock. Asking where they came from could wait until they stopped shaking.

d: Warm your hands before you set out again. A traveller who cannot feel his fingers is in no state to trust a rope.

afterGift: Torvald's lantern will keep its light. It cannot tell you whether the floor ahead is sound.

halvard: I do not remember a different king. I would like to know whether grown people always checked the door before speaking.
I have questions about what comes next. It is strange how much easier it is to ask them when nobody tells me to hush.
history: Why we save the thaw water
The first thaw can run away before the ground is ready to hold it. Older neighbours taught us to catch what we could for the gardens.
Is that why everyone watches the eaves?
Some are thinking of gardens. Some simply want proof that winter can end.

halvard: The levy takes good cider and leaves me explaining the short barrels. I would rather disappoint the king than my neighbours, but he sends armed men to complain.
I have saved a barrel for the people who helped with the apples. This time the first toast belongs to them.
I have walked enough roads to know fear does not end at a town boundary. Halvard has made strangers suspicious of the very people who could help them.
On my next journey I would like to ask for directions without first proving I am harmless. Perhaps that will take time.
The royal songs leave no room for anyone who carried the wood or buried the dead. Those are the verses I listen for.
We need songs that remember the cost as well as your victory. I would not thank you properly by making it sound easy.
I found a coin with his face rubbed smooth. Nobody wanted it less. I thought that was rather telling.
I will keep that worn coin. I like the thought that all those ordinary hands lasted longer than his face on it.
He calls these hunting grounds his. I have yet to see him bring a meal to anybody whose traps were confiscated.
I want families to eat without hiding the pot when someone knocks. Rowan will still hear from me if he takes more than we need.
I have repeated tales just because an official-looking page said they were true. Halvard benefits from people being embarrassed to admit that mistake.
I am checking the stories I passed along. I owe the people who believed me corrections, not a claim that I always knew better.
Fear keeps people away from a healer until a small injury becomes a bad one. A kingdom run that way is expensive in things no treasury counts.
Wren will have work enough without people hiding their wounds. I hope we can make asking for help feel ordinary again.
He is happy to let people fear a witch while his own men take their stores. Maelis has helped more sick neighbours than any proclamation ever did.
I would like us to stop needing someone to blame for every misfortune. Removing Halvard will not cure that habit on its own.
The official histories give him every success and somebody else every failure. Even a bad novelist would vary the plot.
We must keep his proclamations beside the accounts that contradict them. Otherwise somebody will say we exaggerated because we won.
Orders for fine windows travel faster than requests for repairs. I suppose a king need never look through a cracked pane.
Sela's scraps can mend quite a few things. I would like our next busy season to leave more homes sound, not more halls grand.
An extra royal order keeps the hammers going and the apprentices too tired to learn. Work is welcome. Being worked into the ground is something else.
I hope we learn what a normal shift sounds like. Young hands ought to have something left in them after the hammer stops.
The crown takes a share of the catch even when the net needs replacing. A man who has never mended one can be generous with other people's work.
I have promised to teach two neighbours to mend their own nets. We will need more than a change of ruler to look after ourselves.
history: The harbour's shared work
When a boat was overdue, neighbours checked the shore together. Even rivals needed enough hands to mend nets before the next tide.
Did that end their quarrels?
Usually until the boat came back. Helping someone need not mean agreeing with them about everything.

halvard: I can postpone buying a lamp. People who cannot afford bread have nothing left to postpone. That is who I think of when the levy rises.
I would like everyone to have a little money for something they simply like. Keeping people alive should not be our highest ambition.
The town keeps time by its work. His collectors always arrive as though we have been sitting idle waiting to pay them.
It would be pleasant to mark a year by new apprentices and weddings. I am tired of remembering it by increases in the levy.
He wants admiration from people he has frightened. I cannot understand mistaking one look for the other.
I can put a little glass dragon in my window now. It should never have required courage to like a beautiful thing.
I have shared a live coal with neighbours who could not buy fuel. I would like the king to explain why that is left to us.
I will keep carrying the morning fire. A kinder town still takes neighbours getting out of bed to help one another.
My husband comes home too tired to finish supper, and the crown asks why the carts are late. That question tells me enough about Halvard.
He stayed awake through supper yesterday. I would like more evenings like that before anybody asks what else we can sacrifice.
He calls the mines the wealth of the realm. Strange how little of that wealth remains on the streets covered in its dust.
I want the people washing coal out of their sleeves to have a say in where the earnings go. We have been invisible long enough.
There is no royal order for cleaning the dust from a child's bed. That part of the work is apparently beneath notice.
I am glad the banners have changed. I will be happier when cleaner water and shorter shifts follow them.
The night shift grew longer while the promises stayed the same length. I no longer believe a better winter is always one more cart away.
A quiet forge should mean people are resting, not that families have lost their living. We need to find our way to that.
I pack extra food because a crew can be kept below past supper. Halvard's share never seems to wait until morning.
I hope the crews can come home when they say they will. I would like to set the table without listening for trouble.
A blast loosens our windows, but the crown's men say repairs are our affair. They become very interested in responsibility when it belongs to someone else.
If the mine prospers again, some of the money ought to hold the houses together. I have enough old screws to make my case.
You can complain about a leaking roof until someone fixes it. Complain about the king and people ask you to lower your voice. I object to the difference.
Now I can complain at a sensible volume. Flint says he had hoped liberation might be quieter. He should have known me better.
I save each ember while his collectors tell us to give more. There comes a point when careful living cannot cover another man's waste.
We can use the wood we saved for our own winter. Quarrel has already made a list of people who need a share.
I remember neighbours gathering without wondering who might repeat their words. Halvard has taken ordinary ease from people who never threatened him.
I would like a gathering with music and no one posted at the door. Nan still knows the steps, whatever she tells you.
An officer rode a horse here with a torn strap and demanded I fix it at once. The king's mark was apparently meant to hurry the stitching.
A hurried repair can kill somebody. I hope we remember that rank is no substitute for listening to someone who knows the work.
I have spent too many years being careful about a man's name in my own kitchen. You deserve a life where fear of the king is not an ordinary household chore.
You have done enough to earn some quiet, love. People will keep asking things of you. You are allowed to say you need to come home.
history: Growing up in Millwood
When I was little, a visit from Thornwell meant somebody would stay for supper. News took time, so people made room for the person carrying it.
Did everyone know everyone?
No, love. That was why we asked them to sit down.

halvard: I left Thornwell looking for a little peace. Halvard's demands travelled the same roads I did. Moving does not put you outside a king's reach.
Perhaps I can visit the neighbours I left behind. I would like the journey to be a visit this time, instead of an escape.
I like danger in books because I can close them. His rule has made people afraid in rooms that ought to feel safe.
Perhaps adventures will become something people choose again. I intend to enjoy most of mine from this chair.
If I took from the hives the way he takes from the village, there would be no bees next spring. I wonder who taught him to count.
I will still leave enough honey for winter. The end of a levy is an opportunity to recover, not an excuse to strip everything bare.
People arrive here pretending they are merely cold. Sometimes they have been questioned on the road and need to sit where nobody demands an answer.
I will keep the chair by the fire. Coming through hard years can leave a person tired long after the reason is gone.
He measures the seam by what leaves in carts. I measure it by the dust my husband coughs into a cloth.
I want the crews heard before we celebrate how much the mines can produce. We already know what it costs to ignore them.
A royal buyer rejected half a firing over the colour, then offered to take it cheaply. I have not mistaken power for good judgement since.
I can sell a bowl without worrying whether somebody dislikes a colour on behalf of the crown. That is a surprisingly good feeling.
His messengers bring a single account and call it certainty. I want dates, witnesses and a second set of figures.
The records need checking while people still remember them. A new seal at the top of a page will not make a lie true.
history: Reading a town's history
An account book can show a bad harvest without mentioning the weather. A sudden change in grain prices is a question worth taking to other records.
Is that better than a storyteller?
Different. The figures can tell you what changed. A person may tell you what it felt like to live through it.

halvard: He orders work through the noon heat from a shaded room. I would listen more politely if he came out and stood beside us.
I hope those making decisions will ask why we close the shutters at noon. Some customs are experience, not stubbornness.
I mend the straps of travellers frightened to stop long enough for a proper repair. The patrols make the road harder on everyone.
A woman waited while I finished both seams today. Nobody had warned her to move on before a patrol came.
I keep water within reach of every guest. His men once asked why I did not require their names first.
A thirsty person can drink here without answering questions. I would like that to be too ordinary for anyone to remark on.
I avoid names on parcels when a family asks me to. Think of the work that goes into making a gift look like nothing worth inspecting.
I can write my sister's name plainly on the next parcel. She will probably notice that before she notices what I sent.
My grandmother put our family's route into a rug. Halvard can rename a road; he cannot make me unlearn her pattern.
I want to teach the pattern to someone young enough to have walked those roads without fear. Then they can add their own turns.
history: Sandspire's woven maps
Some families worked wells and turns in the road into their borders. The pattern helped children remember a journey before they made it.
Could I navigate by one?
Only with someone who knows the pattern. A rug is a reminder, not permission to walk into the dunes unprepared.

halvard: A trader who changed the bargain as often as Halvard changes a levy would have no customers left. He has soldiers instead.
I would like the next agreements written where everyone can read them. Trust lasts longer when neither side has to guess the terms.
After sunset we bring our chairs outside, but we still look around before mentioning him. He has managed to intrude even when nobody invited him.
We argued about him in the street last night. Nobody agreed on everything, and nobody asked us to stop. I rather enjoyed that.
I keep the crown's charges in their own column. It is useful to know how much of a hard year was weather and how much was a decision.
I am not tearing out that column. If we remember the figures, the next official will find it harder to invent a kinder past.
The sea wears at this house honestly. It never claims to be protecting me while taking another piece.
We still need sound doors and winter stores. I hope the people who promise a better coast begin with those.
history: Building for the coast
Old houses turn their sheltered sides toward the worst weather. You can see where builders learned from the mistakes of the house next door.
And the salt still gets in?
Always. Local wisdom mostly tells you which repairs to expect, not how to escape them forever.

halvard: I can read bad weather. A collector with a smile gives less warning and usually costs more.
I will take an honest storm over another polite demand from Cinderhold. At least now there is only the weather to grumble about today.
A patrol nearly knocked me off that step once and blamed the wet stone. I have heard that manner in every royal notice since.
I would like an apology from someone who means it. Until then, I am keeping the step dry for visitors who mind where they put their feet.
When a boat is late, I worry about the weather and the king's men. One would be enough for a lifetime.
There is one less reason to fear a late sail. The sea will give me plenty without Halvard's help.
We repair our roofs while his halls receive new stone. I wonder how many quiet suppers a grand entrance is worth to him.
I hope the first building plans concern houses people actually live in. We have waited long enough for dry beds.
I am frightened enough of the graveyard. A living king ought to make the rest of the road feel safer, not give me another reason to bolt the door.
I still shut the door at dusk. I might stay outside a little longer beforehand, though. That seems a fair beginning.
I make the broth stretch because people arrive with less coin each winter. Halvard's collectors never ask who went without.
I would welcome a winter when everyone can bring something to the pot. Until then, I will keep making room.
The royal men saw damp ground where we saw a nursery. They wanted it cleared before asking what lived there.
We have kept the nursery. I hope the next people who come here ask us to show them around before drawing a boundary.
We leave young shoots so there will be food later. His people call anything left growing a missed harvest.
Now we have room to let the beds recover. I would rather promise you a harvest next year than boast about a feast today.
When a customer mentions the royal household, I brace for a complaint I am not allowed to answer. Buying a cup should not work that way.
I can ask every customer the same questions now. What do you need, what do you like, and can you carry it home safely?
I have been saving for a glass flower while the levy takes a little more each season. I resent how often a small pleasure becomes something to postpone.
Perhaps I will finally buy the flower. I do not need a grand monument to remember that life can become kinder.
He finds my reputation useful. People frightened of a woman in the marsh ask fewer questions about armed men on their own doorstep.
Do not expect every frightened story to die with him. People will need practice asking each other what actually happened.
history: Why people settled near the marsh
Water, reeds, fish and useful plants brought people here. Fear came later, and made an ordinary livelihood sound like a sinister choice.
Are the frightening stories all false?
No. The marsh has real dangers. An invented one can keep you from recognising the danger under your next step.

d: A ward is useful, but it will not make a reckless traveller wise. I also sell bombs, if you need them for the road.

halvard: His preferred history has no witnesses who can disagree. Keeping the other accounts is the most useful objection I can make.
We must preserve the lies as well as expose them. Future pupils deserve to see how a false account was made convincing.
history: What happened at Wingfall?
Before Wingfall, seven Dragonriders kept the peace. Halvard was one of them. Fifty years ago he turned against the other six and claimed the throne.
Why do the books disagree?
Royal accounts call the others traitors. Older records describe the same people as protectors. Read who wrote an account, and when, before trusting its judgement.

halvard: A report can call lost miners a delay in production. That tells you whose comfort the king wants the reader to consider.
I want to collect the families' accounts while they can still correct us. Names should come before totals for once.
He speaks of glory as though nobody has to tend the graves afterward. I find the omissions difficult to forgive.
We should learn the names of those who never saw this day. Celebration and mourning need not cancel each other out.
I cross out words in my own stories because they do not fit. He crosses out people's accounts because he dislikes what they reveal.
I can let a character disagree with a ruler without hiding the page. I had not realised how much that would change what I wanted to write.
A lesson in which the answer must always praise the king teaches obedience, not thought. I ask my pupils how they know a thing.
Now we can ask the difficult questions aloud. I will still insist they support their answers; freedom is not a reason to stop thinking.
history: How the towns depended on each other
Millwood sent grain along roads that brought back Thornwell fruit and Forgewick tools. Sandspire's caravans and Coralmere's boats carried things no single town could make.
So no town really stood alone?
Exactly. Even the people who never travelled lived partly by strangers' work.

halvard: The temples were here before his crown. I think that is why he dislikes people examining them closely.
The ruins still need careful study. I do not want us replacing his convenient stories with convenient stories of our own.
I want to ask why his authority depends on us never asking how he acquired it. Iven says to keep the question, even when I have to choose my moment to speak.
I would like a ruler whose work we can examine without first reciting praise. That seems a reasonable place to start.
He sends new accounts of Wingfall to the school and expects us to put the old ones away. I do not trust a history whose first instruction is to stop comparing it with anything else.
Keep the versions side by side. Otherwise the person who rewrote them can claim we misunderstood the change.
I study places I am afraid I will never safely reach. It is hard to be grateful to a king for roads you cannot use.
I want to see the coast before making another map of it. For the first time that sounds like a plan, rather than a wish.
His men listen at tables and call it keeping the peace. People come here to put down a day's worries, not acquire new ones.
My customers are beginning to speak at their ordinary volume again. I had forgotten just how noisy a comfortable room can be.
history: Travellers and the Copper Cup
The room grew around travellers needing a place to sit. News passed from table to table long before anyone agreed which version was true.
How did you choose what to believe?
I asked who had actually been there. A full cup improves a story more reliably than it improves the facts.

halvard: You learn to stop pouring when a conversation suddenly goes quiet. Usually a uniform has come through the door.
I am hearing arguments about cider again. Remarkably stupid arguments. I have missed them more than I expected.
I carry letters written as though somebody else will open them. Families deserve to speak plainly to one another.
There is room in a letter for hopes again. I would like to carry more invitations and fewer careful little assurances that nobody should worry.
history: The old letter routes
A carrier would leave a bundle with someone trusted, who passed it to the next traveller heading the right way. The routes depended on people remembering their promises.
Did many letters get lost?
Enough that families numbered them. An account of the past can have missing pages because somebody's pack got wet, not because someone meant to hide them.

halvard: His men can demand another drink on the crown's account. I still owe for mine. Even I can see something wrong with that arrangement.
Bess says freedom has not cancelled my tab. A cruel blow, though I suppose a fair one.
I have watched good workers grow afraid of a knock at the door. I do not care how fine his speeches sound after that.
We should remember who helped their neighbours when it was difficult. A new reign ought to begin with better examples than a crown alone.
If you want my opinion of Halvard, ask when my head stops pounding. I would like the complaint to be properly considered.
He is gone? Good. Wake me for breakfast. I intend to enjoy at least one ordinary morning without discussing a king.
I have served men who confused a silent room with agreement. Halvard has built a kingdom around that mistake.
There are soldiers who need to answer for their actions. There are also frightened recruits who need somewhere better to begin. We must tell the difference.
A king who chooses the rules, deals the cards and punishes anyone who leaves is not winning an honest game.
Let us agree the rules before anyone sits in his chair. I have had enough of finding out what the stake was after losing it.

gift: Fen: Two dancers have to look after each other. I reckon it is the same for you and your dragon.
Fen: Take the Twin Heart. Wear it, and once in a fight your dragon can take a blow meant for you.
Fen: Yes. So look after him too. Two hearts, remember?
afterGift: Fen: Keep looking after each other. That is how you stay in step.
halvard: His patrols make a room forget it was enjoying itself. I keep dancing partly because somebody ought to remember.
I can dance without counting uniforms at the door. I may wear out Bess's floor making up for lost evenings.
I will risk a copper on cards. I will not wager someone else's safety on a king promising that this time he has taken enough.
The future finally feels uncertain in a way I can welcome. I would still advise keeping some breakfast money.
Halvard would be barred from this table. Even I explain a rule after someone catches me changing it.
Grusk says we are playing honestly tonight in honour of the occasion. He seems to think looking directly at me improves the announcement.
A decree calls a pass secure, and a traveller goes missing in it. I trust the people who came through more than the people who sent them.
I want fresh reports before calling any road safe. Your victory matters too much to waste it by pretending every danger vanished with him.
He can demand new words to an old tune. He cannot decide what people remember when they hear the first few notes.
I am writing down the old verses before they slip away. Surviving in whispers should not be the only way a song survives.
history: Songs before the royal verses
Families kept their own words to the same tunes. A wedding verse might turn into a work song two villages down the road.
Was there an original version?
Somebody probably thought theirs was. Shared songs rarely stay the property of the first singer.

halvard: I worry about playing the wrong song before I worry about playing it badly. That is a miserable order for a musician's worries.
I would like to be nervous because people are listening carefully. It is a much better sort of fear than wondering who might report the tune.
I prefer quiet work. Halvard seems to regard anyone doing something he does not understand as an accusation.
I hope we can be left to harmless eccentricities again. A large hat need not conceal a conspiracy.
My sister checks the written facts. I listen to what people will only say after looking over their shoulders. His history fails both tests.
We should compare the records with the people who lived through them. Relief is not a reason to let anyone tidy away the awkward parts.
A conjurer asks the audience to enjoy a deception. Halvard expects them to live inside it and thank him.
I want the clever words examined closely before we applaud whoever comes next. We have paid enough for an impressive performance.
Guests ask whether I keep a list for the soldiers. An inn should be somewhere you can sleep without rehearsing an explanation for being there.
A family booked two nights instead of leaving before dawn. I hope that becomes too ordinary for me to remember.
He orders weapons, then wonders why every grievance ends with steel. I would rather spend my skill keeping people whole.
There will be tools to mend and young smiths to teach. I look forward to making things whose success is measured in years of use.
history: Forgewick's craft
Ore alone did not make Forgewick. Smiths needed fuel, food, water and people willing to learn difficult work from one another.
Did the workshops cooperate?
They argued constantly. Then somebody needed a second pair of tongs and went next door.

d: Keep the blade clean and check your armour straps after a hard fight. Good gear still needs looking after.

halvard: I learned to make protection because people were being hurt. Halvard has been generous with opportunities to test my work.
I would like the next difficult thing I make to be beautiful and entirely unnecessary for surviving a journey.
history: How glassmaking took root
Dunstan and I grew up around Forgewick’s furnaces. My brother took to metal. I came to Sandspire for the glassmaking sand and the caravan trade.
Do smiths ever help you?
My brother sends tools and furnace fittings from Forgewick. I send him glass. Dunstan would be unbearable if I called that artistic collaboration.

halvard: His demands arrive before the apples are ripe, as though a tree might hurry for a royal seal. Joss and I do what we can with the season we get.
I am keeping enough good apples to share with Nan. I would like to plan a winter by who is coming to supper.
The official accounts keep telling us what everyone believed. My notebook is full of people who apparently failed to believe it.
I want to write down the disagreement while we can hear it. A free country should not need every remembered voice to sound the same.
history: The lives between the dates
Histories often skip from one ruler to the next. Letters and household lists show people carrying on through those grand dividing lines.
Does that change the history?
It gives the dates people to happen to. A victory means more when you know who was waiting for news.

halvard: My grandfather's tools made useful things. Too many of the orders coming from Cinderhold begin by asking how much damage something can do.
I have an idea for a better tool chest. It is pleasant to consider a new project without wondering whether someone will order it turned into a weapon.
I watch the road for family. His men watch it for people to stop. We have very different ideas of a useful day's watching.
I am hoping to recognise more faces on that road. Even an unremarkable visit would feel like something restored.
I tie knots for people who have to trust them at sea. Halvard makes promises as though nobody will ever have to put weight on one.
I would like future promises checked as carefully as a working net. Find the weakness before someone is depending on it.
We stack wood before winter. The crown demands its share afterward. I would like the people making that decision to spend a night in the coldest house.
We can count what we need without subtracting a demand we cannot refuse. I hope nobody here has to burn a good chair this winter.
He treats the riders' inheritance as something he can own by denying it to others. Knowledge kept only for a ruler is a poor inheritance.
Guard what you have learned from becoming another ruler's private power. The temples were meant to carry knowledge beyond one lifetime.
history: Why the temples preserve knowledge
A rider's life ends. What they learned need not end with them. The temples gave later riders somewhere to find what their predecessors had kept.
Did they all teach the same things?
They preserved different parts of an inheritance. Learn carefully; possessing a stone is not the same as understanding its use.
afterLightning: You have the Lightning Heartstone now. Learn how Aurelius answers it before reaching for more power.
Good. The temples keep knowledge for riders; they do not spare riders the work of learning.

halvard: A royal wagon gets the road cleared first, no matter whose wheel has broken. I have lost days waiting beside loads that could not afford the delay.
I would like repairs decided by who needs help. A little common sense would keep more carts moving than a grand escort ever did.
roadwork: The wheel is sound and the road is clear. I have checked every pin twice.
With sensible loads and a little care. The sensible loads may prove the harder part.
bramble: Bramble came nosing around my tools earlier. Take him to Rowan at the Copper Cup, north through Thornwell. His owner should be there by now.

halvard: The crown asks why we clear a fall so slowly. I would rather hear complaints above ground than lose Nerik under a hurried repair.
We will still move the dangerous stones carefully. I hope the people writing the schedules have finally learned to ask the crew.
roadwork: The carts are shifted and the bank is stable. We checked the high stones before letting anyone through.
Yes. Leave room for loaded carts; a clear road still needs people looking where they go.

halvard: I am new enough to be told what to do and old enough to see when it is foolish. Marn has kept me safe when an order would not.
I want the next new miner to learn the work without first learning which orders might get him killed.
roadwork: That is the last cart out of the way. Marn made me check the bank once more before putting the tools down.
Nothing moved. I am learning that an uneventful inspection is a very good result.

halvard: I make snow families because I miss people. Halvard's roads have given too many of us a reason to understand that.
Perhaps next winter my brother can help build his own likeness. I will have to find him a less flattering carrot.
history: Winter visitors
When roads closed, people made little figures of the relatives who could not come. That is the custom my family taught me, anyway.
Does everyone here do it?
Not everyone. A family habit can be worth keeping without pretending it belongs to the whole town.
roadwork: The snow family is safely out of the way. Travellers can get through without stepping over anybody's nose.
Perhaps a little dog. Somewhere that does not require another road closure.

halvard: I knew your father when people could disagree in the square without an officer wanting names. I am tired of pretending that is too much to ask.
I have lived long enough to see the square become ours again. Sit a while, Corin. I would like to enjoy that with you.
history: The orchards of Thornwell
An orchard takes years before it gives much back. The people who planted the oldest trees knew someone else might eat most of the fruit.
Do you know their names?
A few. I wish we had written down more of them while there was someone left to ask.

dd: Keep your companion clear of the cider, Corin. I would rather not find out whether dragons like apples by losing a barrel.
dd2: There is space beside the orchard path for him to rest. Mind the young trees.

halvard: His patrols pass my empty beds and call the road prosperous. Perhaps they count the horses instead of the guests.
Both camps could use a season of busy fires. I would rather compete over the stew than wonder whether anyone is coming at all.
His officers want the deep galleries opened. They have not stood at that door and listened. I have.
We can decide what is safe before somebody promises another shipment. I will not miss having that decision made from a warm hall.
Young people leave, old people wait, and his notices say everything is thriving. I would like one written by someone who stays long enough to notice.
I hope some of the young ones come back for a visit. They need not settle here to let us know they are alive.

d: Not many young travellers stop to speak here. Most are already looking farther down the road.
Corin: Where are they going?
Hask: Somewhere they hope will be different. I wish more of them wrote home.
dd: A dragon in the square. I thought I had reached the age when this town could no longer surprise me.
dd2: Keep his tail clear of the benches, lad. Some of us need a moment to stand up.

halvard: I have sat through enough of his reign to recognise a new demand dressed in an old promise. This bench has heard most of them.
I expected to wear out before his reign did. For once I am delighted that my judgement was poor.

dd2: There are people who would report a dragon before asking whether it had harmed anyone. Choose your company carefully.

halvard: The wagons pass with royal seals and nobody will explain the work. People who trust their workers do not keep every order a mystery.
I would like to know what I am loading and who it is meant to help. A plain answer would improve my opinion of government considerably.

d: Royal wagons go north with their covers tied shut. I am asked to handle the empty carts afterward, never to see the loads.
Corin: Do you know what they carry?
Marek: No. And I distrust anyone who insists that means there is nothing worth asking about.
dd: Keep your dragon away from the royal wagons. I do not know what they carry, but I would rather you did not become part of the answer.
dd2: Watch for royal escorts farther along the road. A quiet cart can hide work somebody does not want witnessed.

halvard: His men ask for fuel as though winter is an excuse we invented. The forest will not replace a season's cutting because a king commands it.
We need to let the cut ground recover. Being able to refuse another demand may save more lives than anyone will count.
A king who sends men into dark workings should care whether they come back. I learned to expect that concern from fellow miners instead.
I want the lost men remembered by name. A new tally at the pithead is no answer to the families who kept waiting.

d: The road south can be hard going. Before you explore the Forgewick mines, make sure you have a light you can depend on.

afterGift: The deep workings still deserve caution, even with a steady lantern. Leave yourself a clear way back.

halvard: I have warmed people turned back by a patrol when the storm was already coming. No argument about the king's rights makes that right.
There will be a place by the fire for anyone coming home. We have spent long enough practising how to let people in quietly.
I count houses, graves and how many bowls I can fill. None of his proclamations has improved those numbers.
I would like this town to grow for cheerful reasons. Children, visitors, another table needed at supper. We are owed some ordinary years.
I came outside to study people and learned how quickly they change the subject when a patrol appears. That seems a poor recommendation for a king.
I have begun writing down what people say without lowering their voices. It is a much livelier collection of notes.
The collectors weigh our grain carefully. I wish they were half as careful about leaving enough to feed us.
We can keep enough grain for the winter now. I would like the hens to appreciate how much worrying that saves me.
